raw_case_text:
A 4-year-old male presented to our attention referring left submandibular swelling accompanied by odynophagia and left flexion of the head, in absence of rhinitis or nasal obstruction. The patient was taken to the emergency room where blood chemistry tests were performed showing an increased level of WBC, CRP, and fibrinogen and normal levels of ALT, AST, and LDH. The SARS-COV-2 nasal swab test resulted negative. The neck ultrasound revealed multiple increased size lymph nodes in left II, III, and IV areas, with well recognizable hilum and no colliquation areas. The clinical examination highlighted a laterocervical mesoadenia and inspection of the oral cavity showed tonsils asymmetry (left > right), lateral oropharynx wall swelling and nasopharynx purulent discharge.
CT scan was performed in the clinical suspicion of parapharyngeal abscess, showing nasopharyngeal airspace asymmetry and multiple oval lymphadenopathies along the laterocervical stations bilaterally. Having evaluated both the clinical and radiological evidence, the multidisciplinary team decided to avoid surgery and proceed with IV antibiotic therapy.
In view of an echographic increase in the lymphadenopathies size after medical therapy, a neck MRI was performed under sedation, confirming the persistence of obliteration on the left deep parapharyngeal and carotid spaces with left retropharyngeal lymphadenopathies (Figure 1).
The hospital's diagnostic protocol for pediatric lymphadenopathies was therefore applied, performing multiple tests to identify possible pathogens (blood culture, nasal secretion culture, intradermal Mantoux reaction, and serologies for EBV), which gave negative results.
Serology for Bartonella henselae resulted weakly positive (1 : 256) and the patient therefore perform an abdominal US that was within limits. Pharyngeal swab resulted positive for Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes (GABHS).
During the patient's hospital stay, gradual reduction of the left cervical lymphadenopathies was documented, with symptoms abate and improvement of inflammatory indexes, except for persistence of a mild platelets level increase and the patient was then discharged at home with clarithromycin therapy.
After 4 months from the hospital discharge, the patient experienced a laterocervical swelling relapse, with left cervicalgia, stiff neck, trismus, and fever. At the same time, pain and swelling of the hands appeared, with polymorphous rush at the level of phalanx, foot-plant and lumbar region, and unilateral lameness in the absence of osteoarticular swellings. These symptoms then regressed spontaneously after some days. The SARS-COV-2 nasal swab test resulted negative, blood chemistry tests showed an increase in WBC, CRP, platelets, and fibrinogen, while blood cultures and throat swab cultures gave negative results. Concomitantly, a new antibiotic IV therapy was started and continued for 15 days. PCR and serology for Bartonella, Brucella, Borrelia, Toxoplasma, CMV, and Francisella were performed, all resulting negative. The neck US and MRI showed numerical and dimensional increase of the previously known laterocervical lymph nodes, with evidence of colliquation areas and retropharyngeal space asymmetry. No septic or meningeal signs were found at the clinical examination and the MRI did not highlight meningeal pathology, so it was not deemed necessary to assay cerebrospinal fluid.
Fibrolaryngoscopy revealed adenoid hypertrophy and a minimal asymmetry of the pharyngeal region without macroscopic swelling, with maintained airways patency.
Contextually, the patient experienced strawberry tongue (Figure 2), conjunctival hyperemia and heart murmur. For this reason, cardiological evaluation and echocardiogram were performed, documenting coronary arteries dilation, wider at the level of the common trunk and the proximal right coronary artery (Z score 4.7 and 3.7, respectively).
Suspecting a potential KD diagnosis, the patient started the administration of intravenous immunoglobulins and acetylsalicylic acid at an anti-inflammatory dose.
This therapy led to a prompt clinical and radiological response as follows: gradual improvement of the symptoms and the thermal curve, reduction in the caliber of the coronary arteries (Z score of 3.1 for the common trunk, 2.3 for the right coronary artery), reduction in the lymphadenopathies dimension at MRI (Figure 3), improvement of platelets level, and reduction of the CRP.
The patient continued IV antibiotic therapy for a total of 14 days and was then discharged in good clinical conditions on the 20th day after the admission. Three months later the cardiologic control showed no cardiological sequelae and cardioaspirin therapy was stopped.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 4-year-old male presented with left submandibular swelling, odynophagia, and left flexion of the head, followed 4 months later by recurrent laterocervical swelling, left cervicalgia, stiff neck, trismus, and fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 4-year-old male initially presented to the emergency department with left submandibular swelling accompanied by odynophagia and left head flexion. After initial hospitalization and treatment with intravenous antibiotics and discharge on oral clarithromycin, he experienced a relapse 4 months later characterized by recurrent laterocervical swelling, left cervicalgia, neck stiffness, trismus, and fever. Concurrently, he developed transient pain and swelling of the hands, a polymorphous rash over the phalanges, soles, and lumbar region, and unilateral lameness without osteoarticular swelling, which regressed spontaneously after several days.
subjective.past_medical_history: Prior hospitalization 4 months earlier for left laterocervical and retropharyngeal lymphadenitis treated with intravenous antibiotics and oral clarithromycin.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for odynophagia, fever, neck pain, trismus, transient hand pain/swelling, polymorphous rash on phalanges/soles/lumbar area, and unilateral lameness; negative for rhinitis, nasal obstruction, or osteoarticular swelling.

objective.physical_examination: Initial presentation: laterocervical mesoadenia, tonsillar asymmetry (left > right), lateral oropharyngeal wall swelling, and nasopharyngeal purulent discharge. Relapse presentation (4 months later): laterocervical swelling, stiff neck, trismus, fever, strawberry tongue, conjunctival hyperemia, and cardiac murmur; no septic or meningeal signs and no osteoarticular swelling.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial presentation: elevated WBC, CRP, and fibrinogen; normal ALT, AST, and LDH; negative SARS-CoV-2 nasal swab; neck ultrasound showing multiple enlarged lymph nodes in left levels II, III, and IV with preserved hilum and no colliquation; normal abdominal ultrasound; persistent mild thrombocytosis at discharge. Relapse presentation: negative SARS-CoV-2 nasal swab; elevated WBC, CRP, platelets, and fibrinogen; neck ultrasound showing increased number and size of laterocervical lymph nodes with colliquation; echocardiogram showing coronary artery dilation at the common trunk (Z score 4.7) and proximal right coronary artery (Z score 3.7), which improved after therapy to Z scores of 3.1 and 2.3, respectively.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial neck CT showed nasopharyngeal airspace asymmetry and bilateral oval laterocervical lymphadenopathies. Initial neck MRI under sedation confirmed obliteration of the left deep parapharyngeal and carotid spaces with left retropharyngeal lymphadenopathies. At relapse, neck MRI showed numerical and dimensional increase of laterocervical lymph nodes with colliquation and retropharyngeal space asymmetry without meningeal pathology. Fibrolaryngoscopy revealed adenoid hypertrophy and minimal pharyngeal asymmetry with patent airways.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Initial workup showed negative blood culture, nasal secretion culture, Mantoux test, and EBV serology, weakly positive Bartonella henselae serology (1:256), and positive pharyngeal swab for Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes (GABHS). At relapse, blood and throat cultures as well as PCR and serology for Bartonella, Brucella, Borrelia, Toxoplasma, CMV, and Francisella were all negative. Final clinical diagnosis was Kawasaki disease (KD) presenting with cervical lymphadenopathy and coronary artery dilation (with brucellosis and other infectious lymphadenopathies ruled out). Treatment with intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG), anti-inflammatory dose acetylsalicylic acid, and a 14-day course of IV antibiotics resulted in prompt clinical defervescence, reduction of coronary artery Z scores and lymphadenopathy on MRI, and normalization of CRP and platelets. Discharged on hospital day 20; 3-month cardiology follow-up showed no sequelae and aspirin was discontinued.
